title: Automating content approval without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Content approval that does not nag
excerpt: Track a draft, remind the client once, and wait for a yes on a specific version. Do not publish because a timer ran out.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby. Approval is still that pen, even when the reminder is prepared for you.
caption: The pen is still the approval. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does silence count as approval?
faqs.answer: Not by default. Approval is a person accepting a numbered version in a reply you can find. If a contract says silence will count after a set number of days, a person should still warn them in plain words and decide whether to enforce it. A timer that publishes at midnight is how you learn the clause was a mistake.

faqs.question: How many reminders should a draft get?
faqs.answer: One, while the state is still in review and they have not already replied. A reply with changes pauses the chase until there is a new version to see. A second nag is how clients start treating the thread as noise.

faqs.question: Can the workflow apply the client's comments?
faqs.answer: It can store them. A person should read the comment and the result before the client is told the change is done. Even a new phone number needs a human check of the digits.

markdown:
A content approval workflow should move a draft to the client, remind them once in a voice you wrote, and wait. It should not publish because a timer expired, and it should not rewrite their comments into a new version they have not seen. Approval is a person saying yes to a specific version.

Automate the handoff around the draft that is waiting. The machine may record who has the file, which version it is, and when a reminder is due. Keep a person on anything the client will see, anything that would go live or get paid for, and anything you cannot pull back once it is public. Measure the minutes you spend chasing against the minutes you spend checking that the reminder is still true.

## What "waiting on the client" actually means

Name the state in words your studio and your client share. "In review" means they have the version and you are waiting. "Changes asked" means they replied and a person has not finished the next version. "Approved" means they accepted a numbered version, in a reply you can find. "Published" is a later state, and it is not a synonym for approved.

A draft with no owner is how files go stale. One person on your side owns the request. One person on their side is the approver, named in the message. A group inbox is where approval goes to disappear. If several people must agree, say so, and say what happens if they disagree. The workflow tracks that. It does not vote.

Version the file in the name or in the record: the date, or a plain number. The reminder links to that version, not to "the latest," which may have changed since you asked. Approving a moving target is how a client thinks they said yes to one thing and you ship another.

Write the due date as a real constraint or leave it off. "Please approve today so we stay on track" is fake urgency when the date was chosen by the tool. If a campaign, a print slot, or a launch truly closes, a person puts that date in the note and can explain it. If nothing closes, ask without a costume of crisis.

## The reminder you are allowed to send

One reminder is the default. It contains the name of the piece, the version, the link, the question ("Is this version approved?"), and the name of the person who will make the next edit. It does not contain a stack of previous nags, a guilt sentence, or a preview that contradicts the file.

Send it only if the state is still "in review." If they replied yesterday and the reply is sitting unread, the reminder is wrong even when the calendar says it is due. The workflow can check for a reply before it drafts. A person confirms the reply is not the approval itself. Clients write "looks good but change the headline," and a naive keyword on "good" will mark the piece approved. That is an undo you may not get, especially if the next step publishes.

The client will see the reminder. Use a template a person approved, filled with the title and the version from the record. A model does not freestyle a warmer chase. Warmth in this note is brevity and accuracy.

Google's guidance on [creating helpful, reliable people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is about pages, and the same standard belongs on a draft you are asking someone to bless. People-first means the piece is useful to the reader's actual audience, and that you did not produce it mainly to fill a slot. An approval reminder that exists so a calendar stays full will push unfinished work into public. Wait for the yes. A quiet week is cheaper than a correction.

The subject line is part of the reminder. Google's notes on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) explain that a title should be clear and specific, and that vague or stuffed titles serve people poorly. Your subject is a title. "The homepage headline, version 3, ready for your yes or your changes" tells them what to do. "Following up!" tells them nothing, and it trains them to skip you.

## What their reply means

Read the reply as a person. Sort it into one of four outcomes, and let the workflow store the outcome only after you choose it.

- Approved, with the version named. You may proceed to the next step you already agreed, which might still not be publishing.
- Approved with a small change they described. That is not full approval. Make the change, send the new version, and ask again if the change was more than a typo they already specified.
- Changes, without a yes. The state becomes "changes asked." Do not remind them again until they have something new to review.
- A question. Answer it. The clock on the reminder pauses.

Do not let a model apply their comments to the file and send back "all done" without a person reading both the comment and the result. Comments are ambiguous. "Make it pop" is not an instruction a workflow can close. "Change the phone number to this one" might be, and a person still checks the digit. The client should see the new version, not a claim that their note was handled.

If two stakeholders contradict each other, the workflow does not average their comments. A person asks the named approver which direction stands. Averaging is how you publish a page nobody quite asked for, then remind them to approve it.

## Publishing, paying, and other steps that wait

Approval of a draft is not permission to spend their money, and it is not always permission to publish. Separate those gates in the record. A blog post may need a yes on the words and a separate yes on the moment it goes live. An ad may need a yes on the line and a person to turn on the budget. The workflow can show both gates. It cannot pass the second because the first flipped.

Do not auto-publish at the end of a silence. Silence is not a yes. Some contracts try to say that a lack of reply counts as approval after a stated number of days. If you use a clause like that, a person still sends a plain note before the clause triggers, and a person still decides whether enforcing it is worth the relationship. A timer that publishes at midnight is how you learn the clause was a bad idea.

Do not let the reminder include a new price, a new scope, or a threat to bill for the delay. Those are separate conversations. Folding them into a chase email makes the approval about the invoice, and you will get neither a clear yes nor a calm payment.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include the sites and the brand work that produce these drafts, and the small workflows around them. The approval step stays legible: one version, one approver, one reminder.

## Minutes saved against minutes of review

Time the old chase on five real drafts. Include finding the latest file, checking whether they already replied in a different thread, and writing the note so you do not sound sharp. That is the chore.

Time the new path. Confirm the state, confirm the link opens the version you named, read the template once, send or hold. If that review is slower, you automated too much of the sentence and not enough of the filing. Let the machine own the state and the link. Keep the sentence stable.

Count two failures for a month. One is a reminder sent after they had already replied. The other is a piece marked approved that they did not approve. Either failure means a person stays on every release. The minutes only count as saved when those two stay at zero.

Also notice whether clients start replying more slowly after the reminders begin. A single clear note often speeds them up. A sequence of three automatic nags slows them down, because the thread now feels like a queue. If replies get slower, shorten the sequence. You are measuring the relationship, not the send rate.

## A calendar that can be late on purpose

Build the reminder as a draft that appears on the owner's list on the morning it is due. They release it or they snooze it with a reason: "they said Thursday," "we owe them a fix first," "the link is the wrong version." A snooze with a reason is a successful use of the tool. A system that will not let you snooze has misunderstood the work.

Skip the reminder when you are about to send a different, more important note, such as a change to the date or an apology for a mistake in the draft. Two emails before lunch about the same file splits their attention. Send the one that matters. Let the approval ask ride along or wait a day.

Keep the version history where both sides can open it. When they approve version 3, version 2 should not remain the link in an old reminder that still looks current. Update the record. If you publish, point the record at what went live, so next month's edit starts from the truth.

When the draft is a support problem rather than a page waiting for a yes, the handoff changes character. [Automating support triage without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-support-triage-without-losing-the-relationship) is the next piece to read, because a message from a customer may be urgent, and a reminder-shaped workflow will treat it like paperwork.
